The Vaux's Swift (Chaetura vauxi) is a small, insectivorous bird inhabiting coniferous and mixed forests along the Pacific coast of North America. Field studies of its life history reveal that the wet weight at birth for nestlings is approximately 1.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.5 grams], which is quite low even among members of the Apodidae. Initially, however, the freshly laid egg has an initial wet weight of about 1.73 grams [Ww0 = about 1.73 grams], a figure that indicates the egg actually exceeds the immediate post-hatching mass of the neonate. This apparent paradox reflects the fact that the hatchling emerges after absorbing significant yolk reserves and losing some water during the incubation period. Eggs are placed in a half-cup nest adhered to a vertical surface inside a hollow tree or snag, and they are incubated at a steady temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The delay reflects the altricial nature of the chicks, which require sustained brooding from both parents during the first week after emergence.

Growth proceeds rapidly after the initial hatchling phase, and the ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown nestling prior to fledging is 20.2 grams [Wwi = 20.2 grams]. This asymptotic mass is notably greater than the typical adult body mass of Chaetura vauxi, which averages around 18 grams, indicating that nestlings deposit substantial fat reserves to sustain them through the energetically demanding period of first flight and early independence. The elevated nestling mass is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable foraging conditions encountered by newly volant birds, which must learn to capture aerial insects on the wing. Parent birds make frequent provisioning trips throughout the day, delivering boluses of insects to the developing chick. During this phase, the metabolic demands of the growing nestling are high, and the adults work tirelessly to meet them. Observations in British Columbia indicate that the peak weight of 20.2 grams [Wwi = 20.2 grams] is reached at approximately 24 days after hatching, after which the nestling begins to lose mass slightly as it redirects energy toward feather maturation and muscle development in preparation for departure from the nest cavity.

At the species' typical active metabolic body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the maximum annual reproductive rate is realized, though intraspecific variation in clutch size is influenced by female body condition and local insect abundance. The single-brood strategy is consistent with that of other Chaetura species, which typically cannot rear more than one set of young per season due to the extended period of parental care required. Clutch initiation occurs in late May or early June across most of the breeding range, with replacement clutches laid only if the first attempt fails early in incubation. The unusually high initial egg mass of 1.73 grams [Ww0 = 1.73 grams], which represents a relatively large proportion of the female's own body mass, is thought to provide the embryo with ample nutritive reserves for development under the cool, damp conditions typical of coastal forest nesting sites.
